findings.body: canManage() incorrectly returns true for a view-only principal, granting group-management capability to a caller who should only be able to view groups, an authorization over-grant.
findings.failure_mode: Authorization check silently over-grants management permission to a view-level scope holder.
findings.impact: canManage() incorrectly returns true for a view-only principal, granting group-management capability to a caller who should only be able to view groups, an authorization over-grant.
findings.root_cause: canManage() was implemented by copying the canView() scope check (VIEW, MANAGE) instead of narrowing it to MANAGE only.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the scope list passed to hasPermission() in the global canManage() to only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, matching the correctly-scoped canManage(GroupModel) implementation a few lines below.
findings.title: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants manage access based on view-only scope
findings.trigger: A caller who has only the AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW scope permission on the 'all groups' resource type (no MANAGE scope, no MANAGE_USERS role) invokes GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage().
findings.verifier_reason: Line 70 in GroupPermissionsV2.java shows canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds. The VIEW scope should not grant manage capability. Compare with canManage(GroupModel) at line 79 which correctly uses only MANAGE scope. This is a clear authorization over-grant introduced by the patch.

findings.body: Misleading API documentation may cause callers to expect stream semantics (e.g. lazy evaluation, single-use) from what is actually a materialized Set.
findings.evidence: * @return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission.
findings.failure_mode: Interface documentation diverges from the actual method signature, reducing reviewer/maintainer trust in the API docs.
findings.impact: Misleading API documentation may cause callers to expect stream semantics (e.g. lazy evaluation, single-use) from what is actually a materialized Set.
findings.root_cause: Javadoc text describing the return value was not updated to match the Set<String> signature when the method was introduced.
findings.suggested_fix: Update the javadoc to read '@return Set of IDs of groups with view permission.' to match the declared Set<String> return type.
findings.title: Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() incorrectly describes return type as Stream
findings.trigger: A developer reads the javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), whose declared return type is Set<String>, not a Stream.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 145 shows '@return Stream of IDs' but the method signature at line 147 declares 'Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()'. The javadoc incorrectly describes the return type as Stream when it is actually Set.

raw_findings.body: hasPermission() is called with groupResource.getId() (the internal Resource UUID) instead of the resource name (which stores the actual GroupModel id, as created via resolveGroup()/group.getId()); the findByName lookup inside hasPermission therefore never matches the specific group resource and evaluation falls back to the 'all-groups' policy. Additionally the granted set is populated with resource ids rather than GroupModel ids, so it never matches the actual group ids used later (session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)) to filter users by group, silently breaking group-scoped user visibility.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Per-group permission evaluation misses the intended resource and the returned id set contains wrong identifiers, breaking downstream group-based filtering.
raw_findings.impact: hasPermission() is called with groupResource.getId() (the internal Resource UUID) instead of the resource name (which stores the actual GroupModel id, as created via resolveGroup()/group.getId()); the findByName lookup inside hasPermission therefore never matches the specific group resource and evaluation falls back to the 'all-groups' policy. Additionally the granted set is populated with resource ids rather than GroupModel ids, so it never matches the actual group ids used later (session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)) to filter users by group, silently breaking group-scoped user visibility.
raw_findings.root_cause: Confusion between the internal Resource entity id and the resource name field, which actually stores the GroupModel id.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Use groupResource.getName() (which stores the GroupModel id) instead of groupResource.getId() both when calling hasPermission() and when adding to the granted set.
